This facility sits in Middlesex County, New Jersey, near the town of Piscataway, within the same New York City metropolitan corridor of suburban New Jersey that has long hosted back office and data processing operations for major financial institutions. No independently confirmed street address or building name has been documented for this specific location, though the coordinates place it within a stretch of central New Jersey, spanning Middlesex, Somerset, and neighboring counties, that has developed into one of the northeastern United States's denser concentrations of financial sector and telecommunications infrastructure over the past several decades, drawing major banks in search of disaster recovery and data processing capacity outside Manhattan.

Barclays is one of the world's oldest banking institutions, tracing its roots to 1690, when goldsmith bankers John Freame and Thomas Gould began doing business on Lombard Street in London. The bank operated for more than two centuries in various partnership forms before its modern joint stock structure took shape, and it has grown into a global financial services group headquartered in London with substantial investment banking, corporate banking, and technology operations spanning both the United Kingdom and the United States. Barclays significantly expanded its American investment banking footprint in 2008 when it acquired the core North American operations of Lehman Brothers out of that firm's bankruptcy, a deal that brought thousands of employees, trading operations, and associated technology infrastructure needs into the Barclays organization on the US side of the Atlantic.

Firms with that scale of US trading and technology operations typically require dedicated data center capacity outside their primary trading floors, and central New Jersey has been a common choice for banks headquartered in or near New York City for exactly that reason, offering lower costs and ample power availability compared with sites closer to Manhattan, along with fiber connectivity dense enough to support the low latency links trading operations depend on. Beyond that general pattern, no facility specific details, capacity figures, or construction history for this particular Middlesex County site have been confirmed in available public records, and none are asserted here beyond the general, well documented fact of Barclays's large American banking and technology footprint following its post 2008 expansion into the US market.

reading.body:
This facility's published capacity is not available, placing it outside New Jersey's five published data centers but within the state's 48 mapped facilities. Barclays acquired this Piscataway site as part of its 2008 purchase of Lehman Brothers' North American operations, a $330 million deal that included two New Jersey data centers. The operator has not disclosed power or rack capacity for this location on any corporate specification page this site has read.

Without published watts, the campus cannot be ranked against New Jersey's 111.3 megawatts of disclosed capacity, which concentrates in five other facilities. The state's research infrastructure identifies 48 total mapped sites, but most publish no figures. This facility exists in the registry and on OpenStreetMap coordinates, but remains opaque on scale.

For a reader assessing whether this campus matters to AI infrastructure, the answer depends on unpublished data. Barclays' silence on capacity suggests either a legacy banking facility with minimal IT density, a dormant asset, or a deliberate choice not to disclose. No certifications, SLAs, or recent operational markers appear in published sources. Until capacity is disclosed, this site contributes nothing measurable to the AI compute constraint picture.
